title: 34 Understanding the contribution of colostrum microbiota on colostrum metabolomics and calf gut microbiota development
content:
Abstract
Colostrum provides vital nutrients and antibodies that are crucial for calf health and survival. It also contains microbes capable of utilizing these nutrients to produce microbial-derived metabolites, which may complement the cow’s naturally occurring metabolites and influence the growth and health of calves. However, this association remains largely unexplored. The aim of our study is to identify potential colostrum microbes that can colonize and persist in the gut of newborn calves and characterize colostrum microbe-related metabolites. We collected colostrum samples from 25 Holstein heifers with open access to freestall housing and pasture and fecal samples from their individually housed Holstein-Angus crossed offspring from the recto-anal junction on days 4, 7, 14, and 30 after birth. The colostrum and fecal microbiota were analyzed using full-length 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing on an Oxford Nanopore sequencer. The untargeted metabolomics was analyzed using Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry. The results revealed a total of 430 different bacterial species identified in colostrum samples, and 15 species (e.g., Phocaeicola vulgatus, Ruminococcus gnavus, and Tyzzerella nexilis) were shared amongst colostrum and calf fecal samples collected from all sampling time points, with their abundances gradually reducing by day 30. There were 3 distinct clusters that varied in bacterial composition based on beta diversity (P = 0.001). Among those clusters, Streptococcus thermophilus, Lactococcus lactis, and Comamonas testosteroni had the highest average relative abundances, respectively, and was the main factor in the differing diversity clusters. Three colostrum samples from each cluster were selected as a focal group for the untargeted metabolomics analysis. We identified a total of 405 metabolites present in the colostrum samples. The metabolomic profile was not significantly different between the 3 groups (P = 0.8), though several metabolites were identified to be enriched in individual clusters, such as the tryptophan-derived microbial metabolite, 3-indoleacrylic acid, that exhibited the highest abundance in the L. lactis group. Additionally, there were 427 strong correlations (RSpearman > 0.8, P < 0.05) between the colostrum bacterial species and metabolites, with 272 positive and 155 negative correlations. 3-Phenyllactic acid was positively correlated with 4 bacterial species shared between colostrum and calf feces, showing the strongest correlation with Butyricicoccus pullicaecorum (r = 0.84). Indole derivatives, 5-hydroxyindole and 5-Methoxyindole, were also positively associated with Lachnoclostridium sp YL32, another shared bacterial species of colostrum and calf feces. In conclusion, this study provided high-resolution profiles of colostrum microbiota and metabolomics, identifying key microbes in colostrum that may influence its quality through the production of unique metabolites. Additionally, it highlighted persistent microbes that could have long-term impacts on calf gut microbiota. These microbial and metabolite biomarkers have the potential to enhance colostrum quality and composition, ultimately supporting calf health.
